advances: The exact exponential-moment minimum for the kernel \(e^{-|x-y|}\), combined with maximum-weight anchors in the occupied parity classes, gives a general lower bound for the canonical parity energy. Charging each reflected pair and the central singleton at their original weights transfers this bound through logarithmic integral hitting and the accepted root-hitting depth theorem. Every actual convex body has a point of depth at least \(W/[20(n+1)2^n]\), with the sharper parity-dependent and singleton-corrected estimate below. This improves the general denominator \(288(n+1)2^n\) in accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f`; the factor \(n+1\) remains, so this is not a proof of the locked conjecture.

proof:
The function \(R\mapsto e^R/(R+1)\) equals one at zero, tends to infinity, and has derivative \(Re^R/(R+1)^2\), positive for \(R>0\). This proves existence and uniqueness of \(R_A\), including \(R_1=0\).

We first prove (1). For \(x,y\ge0\), direct integration gives

\[
e^{-|x-y|}
=e^{-x-y}+2\int_0^\infty
e^{-(x-t)}\mathbf1_{\{t\le x\}}
e^{-(y-t)}\mathbf1_{\{t\le y\}}\,dt.
\tag{7}
\]

The kernel is bounded by one. For any finite signed \(\eta\), integration of the nonnegative kernel representation against \(|\eta|\otimes|\eta|\) is finite, so signed Fubini is justified. Thus

\[
\mathcal I(\eta)
=\left(\int e^{-x}\,d\eta(x)\right)^2
+2\int_0^\infty
\left(\int_{[t,\infty)}e^{-(x-t)}\,d\eta(x)\right)^2dt
\ge0.
\tag{8}
\]

For \(A=1\), a probability measure with \(\int e^y\,d\mu\le1\) must be concentrated at zero, since \(e^y\ge1\), with strict inequality for \(y>0\). Hence (1) holds. Suppose now \(A>1\) and abbreviate \(R=R_A>0\). The measure \(\nu_R\) has total mass one and exponential moment \((1+\int_0^R e^z\,dz)/(R+1)=e^R/(R+1)=A\). Its potential is

\[
V_R(y):=\int e^{-|y-z|}\,d\nu_R(z)
=\begin{cases}
(2-e^{y-R})/(R+1),&0\le y\le R,\\
e^{R-y}/(R+1),&y\ge R.
\end{cases}
\tag{9}
\]

The two values agree at \(y=R\). For \(y\ge R\), the inequality \(e^{y-R}+e^{R-y}\ge2\) shows that \(V_R(y)\ge(2-e^{y-R})/(R+1)\); for \(y\le R\) this is equality. Consequently every feasible \(\mu\) satisfies

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int V_R\,d\mu
&\ge\frac2{R+1}-\frac{e^{-R}}{R+1}\int e^y\,d\mu(y)\\
&\ge\frac2{R+1}-\frac1{(R+1)^2}
=\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(A)
=\mathcal I(\nu_R).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]

The final equality follows by integrating the first branch of (9) against \(\nu_R\), using its moment computed above. Positivity (8) for \(\mu-\nu_R\) gives
\(\mathcal I(\mu)\ge2\int V_R\,d\mu-\mathcal I(\nu_R)\ge\mathcal I(\nu_R)\).
The feasible measure \(\nu_R\) attains this bound, proving the exact minimum.

Now consider the scalar table. For each occupied parity class \(c\), choose \(\mathbf a_c\in D_c\) of maximum weight. For \(\mathbf I\in D_c\), put \(Y_{\mathbf I}=\tfrac12\log(w_{\mathbf a_c}/w_{\mathbf I})\ge0\). The assumed midpoint inequality gives a positive integer midpoint and

\[
\sum_{\mathbf I\in D_c}\sqrt{w_{\mathbf a_c}w_{\mathbf I}}
\le\sum_{\mathbf I\in D_c}w_{(\mathbf I+\mathbf a_c)/2}
\le W.
\tag{11}
\]

The last inequality uses injectivity of \(\mathbf I\mapsto(\mathbf I+\mathbf a_c)/2\) within this one class. Images belonging to different classes need not be disjoint. This is the maximum-anchor mechanism in the proof of accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f`, used here without discarding any weight band.

Define the finite positive measures \(\mu_c=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D_c}(w_{\mathbf I}/W)\delta_{Y_{\mathbf I}}\) on \([0,\infty)\), and put \(\mu=\sum_c\mu_c\). The sum ranges over the \(k\) occupied classes, so \(\mu\) is a probability measure. Equation (11) gives

\[
\int e^y\,d\mu(y)
=\frac1W\sum_c\sum_{\mathbf I\in D_c}\sqrt{w_{\mathbf a_c}w_{\mathbf I}}
\le k.
\tag{12}
\]

For two endpoints in the same class, \(|Y_{\mathbf I}-Y_{\mathbf K}|=\tfrac12|\log w_{\mathbf I}-\log w_{\mathbf K}|\). Therefore
\(\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)/W^2=\sum_c\mathcal I(\mu_c)\), with the diagonal terms and both endpoint orders included. Expanding the nonnegative terms from (8) yields

\[
0\le\sum_c\mathcal I(\mu_c-\mu/k)
=\sum_c\mathcal I(\mu_c)-\frac1k\mathcal I(\mu).
\tag{13}
\]

Apply (1) to (12), with \(A=k\), and then (13). This proves (2). When \(k=1\), the same argument uses \(R_1=0\) and \(\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(1)=1\); no division by \(R_1\) or limiting convention is required.

We next pass to the original integral hitting scores. The positivity and midpoint statements for actual fiber volumes are supplied by accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f`. In particular, positive endpoint fibers have their Minkowski average inside the midpoint fiber, and the accepted inequality is
\(w_{(\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2}^{1/d}\ge(w_{\mathbf I}^{1/d}+w_{\mathbf K}^{1/d})/2\ge(w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K})^{1/(2d)}\).
Thus every midpoint used in the scalar proof is an actual positive fiber. The compact projection makes the complete actual table finite; fibers of zero volume remain zero throughout. These facts verify all hypotheses for (2).

At a fixed \(\mathbf J\in D\), use the canonical displacement quantities with the center written explicitly:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_{\mathbf J}(v)&=\min\{w_{\mathbf J+v},w_{\mathbf J-v}\},
&\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}&=\{v\in\mathbb Z^n:\alpha_{\mathbf J}(v)>0\},\\
\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)&=\log\frac{w_{\mathbf J}^2}{w_{\mathbf J+v}w_{\mathbf J-v}},
&B_{\mathbf J}^{\Delta}(s)&=\sum_{\substack{v\in\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}\\\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)\le s}}\alpha_{\mathbf J}(v),\\
E_{\mathbf J}&=\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}}\alpha_{\mathbf J}(v)e^{-\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]

Here \(s\ge0\), \(\alpha_{\mathbf J}(v)\) is the displayed-center \(\alpha(v)\) in `03f071403cdfc69f` and `61062ccd228bf31b`, and \(E_{\mathbf J}\) is their discounted score, written \(E_j\) in the former and \(\Psi_{\mathbf J}\) in the latter. It is separate from the scalar function \(\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}\). The sets \(\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}\) are finite and even, the curvatures are nonnegative, and zero occurs once, with \(\Delta_{\mathbf J}(0)=0\) and \(\alpha_{\mathbf J}(0)=w_{\mathbf J}\).

The canonical endpoint-to-midpoint identity of `61062ccd228bf31b` is

\[
\sum_{\mathbf J\in D}w_{\mathbf J}E_{\mathbf J}
=\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w).
\tag{15}
\]

To check the normalization, each ordered same-parity pair \((\mathbf I,\mathbf K)\) corresponds bijectively to
\((\mathbf J,v)=((\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2,(\mathbf I-\mathbf K)/2)\), with \(\mathbf J\in D\). Its contribution is
\(w_{\mathbf J}\alpha_{\mathbf J}(v)e^{-\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)/2}
=\min(w_{\mathbf I},w_{\mathbf K})\sqrt{w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}}
=w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}e^{-|\log w_{\mathbf I}-\log w_{\mathbf K}|/2}\).
This accounts for both orientations and for the diagonal exactly.

The actual-table comparison in `488f0a583886b5fc` gives \(0\le L_E\le G_E\) for every support in (3). Its inequality follows from the actual root-volume bound and weighted arithmetic-geometric mean:
\(d\log(\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{E,\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf I}^{1/d})\ge\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{E,\mathbf I}\log w_{\mathbf I}\).
Hence every logarithmically eligible support is root-eligible at the same cutoff, with unchanged original weights, so \(m_d(\mathbf J,L;w)\ge m_{\log}(\mathbf J,L;w)\).

For each nonzero \(v\in\mathcal U_{\mathbf J}\), the two distinct endpoints form a member of \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\) with coefficients \(1/2,1/2\) and logarithmic cost \(\Delta_{\mathbf J}(v)/2\). The singleton has logarithmic cost zero. Distinct unordered nonzero reflected pairs have disjoint endpoint sets and none contains \(\mathbf J\): an equality of endpoints forces the displacements to differ by sign. Every set hitting the logarithmic family at cutoff \(L\) must therefore contain \(\mathbf J\) and pay at least \(\alpha_{\mathbf J}(v)\) on each eligible unordered pair. Since \(B_{\mathbf J}^{\Delta}(2L)\) contains two orientations per nonzero pair and one central term, the exact singleton correction gives

\[
m_{\log}(\mathbf J,L;w)
\ge\frac{B_{\mathbf J}^{\Delta}(2L)+w_{\mathbf J}}2.
\tag{16}
\]

This is a lower bound for integral hitting at full original weights. Additional barycentric supports can only increase the required hitting mass.

Both hitting families are finite, contain the singleton at cutoff zero, and have nonnegative costs. Their minima exist over the finitely many subsets of \(D\). Each optimized ratio is attained at a support cost, since the numerator is constant between successive costs while \(1+L\) increases. This also verifies directly the attainment assertions used from `488f0a583886b5fc` and `7fa5a28fe1ac6893`.

Finite summation and \(\int_{\Delta/2}^{\infty}e^{-L}\,dL=e^{-\Delta/2}\) now give

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{\mathbf J}+w_{\mathbf J}
&=\int_0^\infty e^{-L}\bigl[B_{\mathbf J}^{\Delta}(2L)+w_{\mathbf J}\bigr]\,dL\\
&\le2\int_0^\infty e^{-L}m_{\log}(\mathbf J,L;w)\,dL\\
&\le2\mathcal B_{\log}^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)
\int_0^\infty e^{-L}(1+L)\,dL
=4\mathcal B_{\log}^{\mathrm{hit}}(w).
\end{aligned}
\tag{17}
\]

All integrals are finite because \(m_{\log}\le W\). The cutoff convention counts every zero-curvature term, including the singleton, throughout the integral. Multiply (17) by \(w_{\mathbf J}\), sum over \(D\), and use (15). The result is
\(\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)+\sum_{\mathbf J\in D}w_{\mathbf J}^2\le4W\mathcal B_{\log}^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)\), proving the first line of (4).

Accepted fact `7fa5a28fe1ac6893` applies to this original convex body with exactly the root costs and integral charges in (3), and gives an attained point of depth at least \(\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)/6\). Combining that conclusion with (2) and the first line of (4) proves its second line. The center, cutoff, and continuous point are chosen before any halfspace. That predecessor's transfer explicitly includes all closed ambient halfspaces, including vertical boundaries with positive mixed volume. Nothing here changes its measure or deletes boundary atoms. Nor does any step require \(D\) to span \(\mathbb R^n\), so positive supports of lower rank, including a singleton, are covered in the original integer dimension.

It remains to prove the uniform numerical coefficient and the asymptotic. The derivative of \((2R+1)/(R+1)^2\) is \(-2R/(R+1)^3\). Consequently \(\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}\) is positive and nonincreasing in \(A\). Since \(k\le2^n\), \(\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(k)/k\ge\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(2^n)/2^n\). This proves the first inequality in (5) by dropping the nonnegative singleton correction from (4).

For \(n\ge2\), one has \(e^{n+1}/(n+2)>2^n\). Indeed \(e>8/3\) from its exponential series, so \(e^3>16\) gives the case \(n=2\), and the ratio of successive quantities \(e^{n+1}/[(n+2)2^n]\) is \(e(n+2)/[2(n+3)]>1\) for \(n\ge2\). Monotonicity of \(e^R/(R+1)\) yields \(R_{2^n}<n+1\). Thus

\[
\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(2^n)
\ge\frac{2n+3}{(n+2)^2}
\ge\frac6{5(n+1)}
\quad(n\ge2).
\tag{18}
\]

The last inequality is equivalent, after multiplication by positive denominators, to \(4n^2+n-9\ge0\), which holds for \(n\ge2\). For \(n=1\), the first six terms give
\(e^{17/10}>\sum_{j=0}^5(17/10)^j/j!=65161907/12000000>27/5=2(1+17/10)\).
Hence \(R_2<17/10\), so \(\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(2)>440/729>3/5=6/[5(1+1)]\). Thus \(\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(2^n)\ge6/[5(n+1)]\) for every \(n\ge1\). Substitution into the middle expression of (5) proves its final inequality.

Finally put \(t=n\log2\). The defining equation is \(R_{2^n}=t+\log(1+R_{2^n})\), so \(R_{2^n}\ge t\). For all sufficiently large \(t\), \(\log(1+2t)\le t\), which gives \(R_{2^n}\le2t\) by monotonicity of \(R-\log(1+R)\). The defining equation then gives \(R_{2^n}=t+O(\log t)\), hence \((1+R_{2^n})/t\to1\). Substituting back yields \(\log(1+R_{2^n})=\log t+o(1)\), proving the first part of (6). Since \((2R+1)/(R+1)^2\sim2/R\), its second part follows.

When \(W=0\), all halfspace masses are nonnegative and the right side of (5) is zero, so any point of the nonempty \(S\) suffices. For positive \(W\), the guaranteed coefficient relative to \(2^{-n}W\) still tends to zero by (6); the locked absolute-constant assertion remains unresolved by this theorem.
statement:
For a finite real \(A\ge1\), let \(R_A\ge0\) be the unique solution of \(e^{R_A}/(R_A+1)=A\), and put \(\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(A)=(2R_A+1)/(R_A+1)^2\). This is the scalar function called \(\Psi(A)\) in the supplied last response; the subscript distinguishes it from predecessor quantities. For a finite signed Borel measure \(\eta\) on \([0,\infty)\), define

\[
\mathcal I(\eta)=\iint_{[0,\infty)^2}e^{-|x-y|}\,d\eta(x)\,d\eta(y).
\]

Among Borel probability measures on \([0,\infty)\) satisfying the exponential-moment constraint, the exact minimum is

\[
\min_{\substack{\mu\text{ a Borel probability on }[0,\infty)\\
\int e^y\,d\mu(y)\le A}}\mathcal I(\mu)
=\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(A).
\tag{1}
\]

It is attained by \(\nu_{R_A}=(\delta_0+\mathcal L^1|_{[0,R_A]})/(R_A+1)\), where \(\delta_0\) is unit point mass at zero. At \(A=1\), this is \(\delta_0\) and the minimum is one. Sharpness in (1) concerns this measure problem, without an assertion that its extremizer is a convex-body fiber table.

For the scalar application, let \(n\ge1\) be an integer and let \(w=(w_{\mathbf I})_{\mathbf I\in\mathbb Z^n}\) be a nonzero, nonnegative, finitely supported table of finite real numbers. Put \(D=\{\mathbf I:w_{\mathbf I}>0\}\) and \(W=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}w_{\mathbf I}>0\). Assume that for every same-parity pair \(\mathbf I,\mathbf K\in D\), its integer midpoint satisfies \(w_{(\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2}^2\ge w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}\). Congruence is coordinatewise. Write \(D_c=\{\mathbf I\in D:\mathbf I\equiv c\pmod2\}\) and let \(k\in\{1,\ldots,2^n\}\) be the number of nonempty \(D_c\). Retain precisely the ordered-pair energy of accepted fact `61062ccd228bf31b`:

\[
\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)
=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf I,\mathbf K\in D\\\mathbf I\equiv\mathbf K\pmod2}}
w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}
\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12|\log w_{\mathbf I}-\log w_{\mathbf K}|\right).
\]

The absolute log difference equals that predecessor's absolute energy difference, so this is exactly its normalization. Then

\[
\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)\ge\frac{W^2}{k}\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(k).
\tag{2}
\]

No log-concave extension or full-dimensionality of \(\operatorname{conv}D\) is assumed for (2).

For the actual-body conclusion, let \(n,d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body, and retain the locked set \(S=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\ne\varnothing\) and its closed-halfspace depth \(h_S\). Use the complete actual table \(w_{\mathbf I}=\mathcal L^d(C_{\mathbf I})\), where \(C_{\mathbf I}=\{\mathbf y:(\mathbf I,\mathbf y)\in C\}\); empty and lower-dimensional fibers have weight zero. Thus \(W=\mathcal H_d(S)\). Assume \(W>0\) until the final zero-volume convention.

The following definitions retain the integral hitting conventions of accepted facts `488f0a583886b5fc` and `7fa5a28fe1ac6893`. For \(\mathbf J\in D\), let \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\) consist of the nonempty affinely independent sets \(E\subseteq D\) for which \(\mathbf J\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}E\), and write \(\lambda_{E,\mathbf I}>0\) for their unique barycentric coefficients at \(\mathbf J\). Define

\[
\begin{aligned}
G_E&=\log w_{\mathbf J}-\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{E,\mathbf I}\log w_{\mathbf I},\\
L_E&=\log\frac{w_{\mathbf J}}
{\left(\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{E,\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf I}^{1/d}\right)^d},\\
m_{\log}(\mathbf J,L;w)
&=\min\left\{\sum_{\mathbf I\in F}w_{\mathbf I}:
F\subseteq D,\ F\cap E\ne\varnothing\text{ for every }E\in\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\text{ with }G_E\le L\right\},\\
\mathcal B_{\log}^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)
&=\max_{\mathbf J\in D,\ L\ge0}\frac{m_{\log}(\mathbf J,L;w)}{1+L}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]

The formula for \(G_E\) is exactly that of `488f0a583886b5fc` after cancelling its common \(\log w_{\max}\). Replacing \(G_E\) by \(L_E\) in the hitting condition defines \(m_d(\mathbf J,L;w)\) and \(\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)\) exactly as in `7fa5a28fe1ac6893`. All hitting charges are the full original \(w_{\mathbf I}\), independent of their barycentric coefficients. Costs are nonnegative, cutoffs use weak inequalities, and the singleton \(\{\mathbf J\}\) has cost zero. All these extrema are attained. Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B_d^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)
&\ge\mathcal B_{\log}^{\mathrm{hit}}(w)
\ge\frac{\mathscr S_{\mathrm{par}}(w)+\sum_{\mathbf J\in D}w_{\mathbf J}^2}{4W},\\
h_{\max}(C):=\max_{\mathbf p\in S}h_S(\mathbf p)
&\ge\frac{W}{24k}\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(k)
+\frac{\sum_{\mathbf J\in D}w_{\mathbf J}^2}{24W}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]

In particular, there is a single \(\mathbf p^\star\in S\), chosen before the arbitrary closed ambient halfspace, such that

\[
h_S(\mathbf p^\star)
\ge\frac{W}{24\,2^n}\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(2^n)
\ge\frac{W}{20(n+1)2^n}.
\tag{5}
\]

The bounds include vertical halfspaces and boundaries containing entire fibers, and impose no rank assumption on the positive support. The dimension-only coefficient in the middle of (5) satisfies

\[
R_{2^n}=n\log2+\log(n\log2)+o(1),
\qquad
\frac{\Psi_{\mathrm{mom}}(2^n)}{24\,2^n}
\sim\frac{1}{12(\log2)n2^n}
\quad(n\to\infty).
\tag{6}
\]

This is an asymptotic for the guaranteed coefficient, not for the actual maximum depth. If \(W=0\), every point of the assumed nonempty \(S\) satisfies (5) with right side zero; the positive-support quantities and ratios in (2)-(4) are not used in that case.
